https://kashmirreader.com/2026/11/26/us-.title: US proposes up to 25% ‘excess capacity’ tariff on India, 17% if trade deal is signed | Kashmir Reader
https://kashmirreader.com/2026/11/26/us-.p1: NEW DELHI: The US on Wednesday proposed 25% tariffs on Indian goods in the absence of a trade deal, citing excess industrial capacity, sustained market access barriers and inadequate labour protection that harm American companies. The US Trade Representative (USTR) said the tariffs on India would amount to 17% if it agrees to a trade deal with America. The fresh tariff proposal follows Section 301 investigations launched by the USTR in March targeting 16 economic jurisdictions. The USTR proposed tariffs of up to 20% to 35% on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place. The EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland face 15 per cent tariff rates, inclusive of standard import duties. Vietnam would face tariffs of 20 per cent if the trade deal is finalised. “For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” said USTR Jamieson Greer. “India generates trade surpluses in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, steel, and ICT goods, revealing dependencies on Indian manufacturing in certain key sectors,” the USTR said in its report on ‘India’s Acts, Policies, and Practices Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors’. These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labour or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior US official said. The USTR has decided to schedule public hearings on its proposals on January 25 and sought written comments from interested persons by January 5. The Office of the USTR has been analysing for several months whether 16 jurisdictions have policies that favour surplus production, a practice that drives down prices and harms US industry. The investigation began last March, after the Supreme Court overturned the indiscriminate trade levies imposed by the Trump administration invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). After that reversal, the USTR opened two investigations based on Article 301: one directed at 60 jurisdictions (about a hundred countries) for violating export regulations on forced labour; and the other against 16 jurisdictions for promoting surplus production. India and the US are negotiating an interim bilateral trade agreement after the framework they had finalised in February went back to the discussion board with the Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA tariffs imposed last year. India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods in the US market than its competitors such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia. “USTR is applying to India a diagnosis built for a very different economy. India consumes most of what it produces and buys more goods from the world than it sells, so it is not exporting a domestic glut,” said Abhik Sengupta, a Task Force Observer on the Committee on Strategic Trade and Market Access, Helsinki Geoeconomics Society. Sengupta said India’s reliance on Chinese inputs points to gaps in its industrial base, not a surplus. “Penalising India for closing those gaps risks pushing supply chains back toward the very economies Washington is most concerned about,” he said. Trump undeterred by midterms defeat Trump reignited global trade tensions on Wednesday by proposing new tariffs on major trading powers including China, undeterred in his protectionist push by losses by his Republican Party in US midterm elections. His administration proposed levies on 14 trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity. The highest rate of 20% would hit China, which Washington blames for flooding world markets with cheap exports of everything from steel to electric vehicles and solar products. “We know that they don’t like these actions, but we are seeking stability with the Chinese. China is seeking stability with us,” a senior US official said, adding Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week was “really great”. Beijing earlier reiterated its opposition to “trade wars” and dismissed the notion of overcapacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation. “The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, urging the world’s two top economies to maintain stable relations. The senior US official said the administration also proposed tariffs on Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. For now, Mexico and Norway are excluded from new levies. The new duties will take into account any trade deals agreed with the Trump administration and will not stack on top of some previous tariff rounds, suggesting many countries may not see a massive increase in the trading cost with the US. Even so, the prospect of new trade burdens weighed on stock markets on Wednesday as a tech-led rally continued to run out of steam. MSCI’s gauge of stocks around the globe fell 0.5%. “It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING analysts wrote. New duties won’t exceed negotiated limits Trump’s tariffs have contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the United States, and a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll following November’s midterm losses for his Republicans showed 62% of respondents would support efforts to repeal them. But Trump has long served notice of a plan to rebuild the duties the US Supreme Court struck down in February. The latest ones come after an eight-month Section 301 unfair trade practices probe. The US official also said the new duties would not exceed tariff limits in any trade deals with the Trump administration, including a 20% cap for China during Trump’s second term under a year-old truce with Beijing that is due to expire on January 10. The tariffs would also not apply to about $30 billion worth of Chinese imports that the US is considering for tariff reductions under a bilateral process, the official said. However, they would add to the tariffs on China put in place during Trump’s first term, which amounted to roughly 25%. The proposed duties will further not stack on top of tariffs of 10% or 12.5% that the administration imposed in July on a wider group of 60 trading partners over allegations of lax enforcement of anti-forced-labor laws. Specific rates are to be published in a US Federal Register notice on Wednesday. Tariff rates also will be consistent with trade agreements signed by other partners, the official said, including the 15% cap agreed by the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, as well as a 19% cap agreed by Malaysia. The proposed duties will be subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing scheduled before they go into effect. The official said that could push implementation into January. PTI/Reuters
